questions.text: Walk me through a production RAG pipeline.
points: Two pipelines, not one — different SLAs, different scaling, different failures
Offline: load → parse → chunk → enrich metadata → embed → index
Online: rewrite → retrieve → rerank → assemble → generate → cite
Seam = versioned contract: embed model + chunk scheme + index + prompt
Caches (embedding / retrieval / semantic answer) = where cost actually goes

questions.flow: offline build ‖ online serve → bound by a versioned contract

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q3: "Sketch the naive RAG pipeline out loud — then tell me the first three places it breaks in production."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Five stages ingest-to-answer. For the breaks: one is before the vector store, one is at query time, one is after retrieval succeeds.
points: Pipeline in one breath: load → chunk → embed → index, then at query time embed query → top-k similarity → stuff prompt → generate.
Break 1 — ingestion/chunking: bad parsing and arbitrary splits mean the right answer never makes it into any retrievable chunk. Garbage in, confidently wrong out.
Break 2 — query-document mismatch: users ask short, vague, conversational questions; documents are long and declarative — raw similarity between them is weak (the asymmetry problem).
Break 3 — blind generation: naive RAG stuffs whatever came back and answers unconditionally — no relevance check, no abstention, no conflict handling.
Frame it as a taxonomy: retrieval failures (missed/wrong chunks) vs generation failures (ignored/contradicted context) — every advanced RAG pattern is a patch on one of these.
drill.oneLiner: Naive RAG is load-chunk-embed-index then retrieve-stuff-generate — and it breaks at parsing, at query-document mismatch, and at generation that never questions what retrieval returned.
drill.followUp: "Which failure class do you fix first?" → Retrieval — generation can't be grounded in context it never received.

questions.text: RAG, fine-tuning, or long context — how do you choose?
points: RAG = knowledge that changes / is large / needs citation
Fine-tune = behaviour, format, tone, domain idiom — not facts
Long context = one document you already hold
Cost shape: RAG per-query · FT once + every refresh · LC every token every call
Real answer usually RAG + tuned embedding model, not tuned LLM

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q2: "A client wants the model to 'know our documentation.' RAG, fine-tuning, or just dump it all into a long context — walk me through the decision."
drill.badge: Trending — recurs across 2026 RAG interview banks + AI-engineer JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Separate knowledge from behavior, then ask three questions about the corpus: how big, how fast it changes, and who's allowed to see what.
points: Fine-tuning teaches behavior, not facts — style, format, domain vocabulary. It's the wrong tool for knowledge: no provenance, stale the day after training, and updates mean retraining.
Long context works for a small, stable corpus — but you pay tokens per query, latency grows with input, and attention degrades over long inputs (lost-in-the-middle), so "it fits" isn't "it works".
RAG wins when the corpus is large, changes often, needs citations, or needs per-user access control — you retrieve only what's relevant and pay for that.
The decision axes to say out loud: corpus size, change rate, provenance requirement, ACLs, latency/cost budget.
Senior move: they compose — fine-tune for tone/format, RAG for facts, long context as the fallback when the corpus is genuinely tiny.
drill.oneLiner: Fine-tuning changes behavior, long context rents knowledge per query, RAG owns knowledge — pick by corpus size, change rate, provenance, and ACLs.
drill.followUp: "Context windows keep growing — does that kill RAG?" → It kills RAG for small corpora; it doesn't fix cost-per-query, permissioning, or attention dilution at millions of documents.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q19: "Fifty million vectors, multi-tenant SaaS product: pgvector, a dedicated vector DB, or FAISS in-process — argue it."
drill.badge: Evergreen — the build-vs-buy proxy war of 2025–26.
drill.hint: Argue from operational shape, not features: who handles sharding, filtering, replication, and the second copy of your data?
points: pgvector: vectors live next to your relational data — one database, real transactions, filters are SQL WHERE clauses, no sync pipeline. The right default for small-to-mid scale; at 50M vectors with high QPS and heavy filtering you're pushing into careful tuning and vertical-scaling territory.

Dedicated vector DB: purpose-built ANN, filter-aware search, horizontal sharding/replication, namespaces for tenancy — but now you own a second data store and the consistency pipeline between source-of-truth and index (the classic dual-write drift problem).

FAISS in-process: a library, not a database — fastest raw search, but no persistence story, no replication, no filtering to speak of, no multi-tenancy; you'd be building a database around it. Right for batch/offline or research, wrong as a multi-tenant serving backbone.

The multi-tenant lens sharpens it: you need filter-aware search + namespace isolation + independent scaling — that's the dedicated store's home turf at this size; pgvector remains defensible if vectors-per-tenant are modest and you shard by tenant anyway.
Decision sentence: choose by operational ownership — who you want paging at 3 a.m.: your Postgres team, a vendor, or the team that built a bespoke FAISS service.
drill.oneLiner: pgvector until scale or filtering pressure proves otherwise, a dedicated vector DB when 50M multi-tenant vectors demand filter-aware sharded search, and FAISS only if I'm prepared to build the database around the library myself.

questions.text: What's asymmetric retrieval, and why does it matter?
points: Symmetric = query and doc same shape (dedup, similar-item)
Asymmetric = short query ↔ long passage — this is RAG's actual case
Model must be trained asymmetric or you lose recall silently
Hence query/doc instruction prefixes in modern embedding models
questions.badge: Evergreen — small mechanic, disproportionate signal.
questions.flow: short query ↔ long passage → needs asymmetric-trained model + prefixes
questions.trap: using a similarity model for search and blaming chunking

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q14: "Why do some embedding models want a 'query:' or 'passage:' prefix — and what silently breaks if you skip it?"
drill.badge: Evergreen — small mechanic, disproportionate signal.
drill.hint: A three-word question and a three-paragraph answer are not the same kind of text. How does the model reconcile them into one space?
points: Symmetric vs asymmetric retrieval: symmetric matches like-with-like (sentence↔sentence, dedup, clustering); RAG is asymmetric — short interrogative queries against long declarative passages.

Asymmetric-trained models learn two conditioning modes and expose them via prefixes or instruction strings — the prefix tells the model which side of the mapping this text is on, so both sides land in a compatible region of the space.
Skip the prefix and nothing errors — you just get quietly degraded similarity scores, the worst kind of bug: retrieval works, ranks are mediocre, nobody knows why.
Instruction-tuned embedders generalize this: the task description is part of the input, so one model serves retrieval, clustering, and classification with different instructions.
Interview flex: this is also why evaluating a model with the wrong usage convention makes a good model look bad in your bake-off.
drill.oneLiner: RAG is asymmetric retrieval — the prefix tells the encoder whether it's embedding a question or a passage, and skipping it degrades ranking silently rather than loudly.

questions.text: Name the ways a RAG system fails.
points: Ingest: bad parse, lost tables, missing docs
Chunk: context severed, subject lost
Retrieve: wrong chunk (recall) or right chunk buried (precision)
Assemble: truncation, lost-in-middle, conflicting sources
Generate: ignores context, hallucinates, won't abstain
questions.flow: ingest → chunk → retrieve → assemble → generate; name the stage first
questions.trap: calling everything "hallucination"

questions.text: How does HNSW work? Why only approximate?
points: Multi-layer navigable small-world graph ≈ skip list in vector space
Top layers sparse/long-range → bottom layer dense/all nodes
Greedy descent from top entry point → local optimum = the "approximate"
Dials: M links/node · efConstruction build · efSearch = runtime recall↔latency
Weak spots: memory-hungry, soft deletes accumulate

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q16: "Exact search vs approximate nearest neighbor — what exactly are you giving up, and how is the loss measured?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Brute force is O(N) per query and perfectly correct. ANN buys speed with what currency, and what's the name of the metric on the price tag?
points: Exact (flat) search compares the query to every vector — perfect results, linear cost; entirely fine up to the low millions on modern hardware, which is a point people forget to say.
ANN pre-organizes vectors (graphs, clusters, quantization) to visit only a fraction — sublinear latency in exchange for possibly missing true neighbors.

The price tag is recall@k against ground-truth exact search: "recall 0.95" means 5% of true top-k neighbors are absent. It's a tunable loss — every ANN index has a search-effort knob trading latency back for recall.
Say the operational consequence: ANN recall loss is a silent upper bound on your whole RAG system — no reranker or prompt can recover a chunk the index never surfaced.
Senior default: start flat/exact; adopt ANN when latency or scale forces it, and re-measure recall after every index parameter change.
drill.oneLiner: ANN trades a measurable fraction of true neighbors for sublinear latency — the recall knob is tunable, but whatever you give up becomes an invisible ceiling on the entire pipeline.

questions.text: HNSW vs IVF vs IVF-PQ — when each?
points: HNSW — best recall/latency, highest RAM, painful deletes
IVF — cluster into cells, probe nprobe cells; cheap build, rebuild-friendly
PQ — compress vectors to codes; big RAM win, recall cost
DiskANN/ScaNN — when index must exceed RAM
Churn + scale push you off HNSW
questions.badge: Evergreen — the index-internals question in every vector-DB interview.
questions.flow: RAM budget? churn rate? → HNSW · IVF-PQ · DiskANN
questions.trap: treating HNSW as the only index

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q17: "HNSW vs IVF-PQ — mechanism, memory profile, and when each wins."
drill.badge: Evergreen — the index-internals question in every vector-DB interview.
drill.hint: One is a multi-layer skip-list-like graph you walk greedily; the other is Voronoi cells plus compression. Which one is RAM-hungry and which one is RAM-thrifty?
points: HNSW: hierarchical navigable small-world graph — greedy descent from sparse top layers to a dense bottom layer. High recall at low latency, incremental inserts, but everything lives in RAM (vectors + graph edges), and deletes are awkward (tombstones, periodic rebuild).
Its knobs: M (edges per node — memory vs connectivity) and efSearch (candidate list — latency vs recall).

IVF: k-means partitions the space into cells; search probes only nprobe nearest cells. Add PQ and vectors compress to bytes — dramatic memory reduction, some recall loss, and the coarse quantizer needs training data upfront; heavy churn degrades centroids over time.
Rule of thumb to say: HNSW when RAM affords it and latency/recall are king; IVF-PQ when the vector count makes RAM the binding constraint; disk-resident designs (DiskANN-style) when even that fails.
Bridge to production: managed vector DBs mostly run HNSW variants under the hood — the knobs above are what their tuning parameters map to.
drill.oneLiner: HNSW is a RAM-resident graph you walk greedily — best recall-latency at a memory price; IVF-PQ buckets and compresses — a memory-cheap index that pays in recall and needs training; the binding constraint picks the winner.
drill.followUp: "What happens to HNSW under heavy deletes?" → Tombstones accumulate and graph quality decays — you schedule rebuilds/compaction.

questions.text: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder — why run both?
points: Bi — encodes query/doc independently → docs precomputed offline → corpus scale, capped accuracy
Cross — joint pass, full cross-attention → accurate, nothing precomputable
∴ retrieve-many-rerank-few: bi pulls ~50–100, cross reorders top few
ColBERT sits between — per-token, precomputable, storage cost

links.label: Why Rerank — Bi Encoder Recall vs Cross Encoder Precision

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q27: "If cross-encoders are so much more accurate, why not use one for retrieval and skip the vector index entirely?"
drill.badge: Trending — bi- vs cross-encoder recurs across 2026 RAG interview banks + AI-engineer JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: What can you precompute for a bi-encoder that is by construction impossible to precompute for a cross-encoder?
points: Bi-encoder: query and document encoded separately → document vectors are precomputable and indexable; query time is one encode plus an ANN lookup over millions.
Cross-encoder: query and document go through the model together, attention across both texts → far finer relevance judgment, but the score cannot exist before the query arrives. Nothing to index.
Using it for search means scoring the entire corpus per query — a forward pass per document; at millions of documents that's not slow, it's architecturally impossible.
Hence the canonical two-stage design: bi-encoder (plus BM25) casts a wide, cheap net; cross-encoder re-scores tens of candidates — recall machine first, precision machine second.

Sharp way to close: the bi-encoder compresses each document into one query-agnostic vector — lossy; the cross-encoder reads the document in light of this query — that's the accuracy gap, and it's exactly what precomputation must give up.
drill.oneLiner: A cross-encoder's score can't exist until it sees the query, so there's nothing to index — you'd run the model over the whole corpus per query; that's why it re-scores a bi-encoder's shortlist instead of replacing it.

questions.text: Hybrid search — why RRF instead of a weighted score blend?
points: Dense = paraphrase/intent · Sparse (BM25) = exact tokens, IDs, error strings, rare nouns
Weighted sum needs two score distributions calibrated — drifts per query/corpus/model
RRF fuses ranks: 1/(k + rank) summed → scale-free, no tuning
Win is largest on identifier-heavy corpora; near-zero on clean prose
questions.badge: Trending — hybrid + RRF recurs on Medium/TDS production-RAG posts + 2026 interview banks (2025–26)
questions.flow: two retrievers → fuse on rank not score → no calibration to maintain
questions.trap: proposing weighted fusion without mentioning calibration drift

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q21: "Why is BM25 still in every serious RAG stack in 2026 — and how does RRF fuse it with dense scores without normalizing anything?"
drill.badge: Trending — hybrid + RRF recurs on Medium/TDS production-RAG posts + 2026 interview banks (2025–26)
drill.hint: BM25's three ingredients fit in one sentence. And RRF's trick: what does it throw away about each ranker's scores that makes them comparable?
points: BM25 = term frequency with saturation (repeats help less and less) × inverse document frequency (rare terms dominate) × length normalization. No training, no drift, interpretable, and exact on identifiers — it covers precisely the dense failure modes from Q20.
The fusion problem: BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on incomparable scales — averaging them is meaningless and normalization is fragile per-query.

RRF sidesteps it by discarding scores entirely: each document earns 1/(k + rank) from each ranker, summed. Only positions matter — scale-free, robust, no tuning beyond the smoothing constant k (which damps the top-rank dominance).

Cost of that robustness: rank-only fusion ignores confidence magnitude — a razor-thin #1 and a runaway #1 count the same; weighted or score-based fusion can beat it when you calibrate, RRF wins when you won't.
Production shape: run both retrievers in parallel, RRF-fuse into one candidate pool, feed the reranker — the near-universal first stage of 2025–26 stacks.
drill.oneLiner: BM25 covers exactly the token-precision cases dense retrieval smooths away, and RRF fuses them by summing reciprocal ranks — comparable by construction because it throws the incomparable scores away.
drill.followUp: "When would you weight one side?" → Corpus-dependent: code/API docs lean sparse-heavy; conversational support corpora lean dense-heavy — set weights from eval slices.

questions.text: Contextual / late chunking — what does it fix?
points: Problem: chunk says "revenue grew 3% that quarter" — whose? which? → unretrievable
Contextual chunking = LLM writes situating blurb, prepended before embedding
Late chunking = embed whole doc with long-ctx model, then pool into chunks
Cost: one LLM call per chunk at ingest — prompt caching makes it far cheaper
Anthropic reported large retrieval-failure reductions, more when combined with BM25 + rerank
questions.flow: chunk lost its subject → restore context before embedding → pay ingest once
questions.trap: confusing the two — one prepends text, one pools embeddings

questions.text: HyDE — what does it solve?
points: Problem: short query and long answer live in different embedding regions
LLM generates a hypothetical answer → embed that → search with it
Closes the asymmetry gap; helps most on sparse/jargon queries
Costs an extra LLM call + can amplify a wrong premise
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: query ≠ answer shape → synthesise fake answer → retrieve with it
questions.trap: using it when a cheap query rewrite would do

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q24: "Explain HyDE in one breath — and when does it backfire?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: It attacks the query-document asymmetry from Q14 — by changing which kind of text you embed. What's the failure mode when the LLM knows nothing about the topic?
points: HyDE: instead of embedding the short question, have the LLM hallucinate a plausible answer document and embed that — a fake passage lands nearer to real passages than a question does. Document-to-document beats question-to-document.
It's the elegant fix for query-document asymmetry: you convert the query into the same text register as the corpus.

Backfires when: the topic is out of the LLM's knowledge — the hypothetical drifts confidently in the wrong direction and retrieval follows it; also adds a full LLM call to the latency path of every query.

Related transform to mention: step-back prompting — abstract the specific question to its general principle, retrieve on that, answer the specific — good when specifics are too narrow to match anything.
Placement note: these are query-side fixes — cheap to A/B because nothing about the index changes.
drill.oneLiner: HyDE embeds a hallucinated answer instead of the question so the match is document-to-document — brilliant on asymmetry, harmful when the model can't hallucinate in the right direction, and it always costs an LLM call of latency.

questions.text: MMR — what is it for?
points: Top-k by pure similarity returns near-duplicates — k slots, 1 fact
MMR = relevance − λ·(similarity to already-selected)
Buys coverage/diversity for multi-aspect and summarisation queries
λ too high → drifts off-topic
questions.flow: dedupe the context window → relevance minus redundancy
questions.trap: confusing MMR (diversity) with reranking (precision)

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q11: "Retrieval keeps finding the right sentence, but the model can't answer because the surrounding context is missing. What patterns fix this?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: The fix is to stop making one chunk serve two masters. What are the two jobs, and which pattern gives each job its own text?
points: Root insight: a chunk has two jobs — being found (wants small and sharp) and being read (wants complete). One text can't optimize both.
Parent-document / small-to-big: index small child chunks for precise matching, but return the parent chunk or section to the LLM. Store the parent link in metadata. This is the workhorse fix.
Contextual enrichment: prepend an LLM-written line situating the chunk in its document before embedding — the chunk carries its own context into the vector.
Late chunking: embed the full document through a long-context embedder first, then pool per chunk — each chunk vector absorbs document-wide context without extra LLM calls.
Sentence-window variant: retrieve the sentence, expand to a window around it at assembly time.
Cost note: all of these raise ingest complexity or index size — again, justified by eval delta, not fashion.
drill.oneLiner: Decouple search granularity from read granularity — match on small chunks, feed the model their parent context, or bake document context into the chunk via contextual or late chunking.

questions.text: ColBERT / late interaction — where does it fit?
points: Per-token embeddings, not one vector per doc
Scoring = MaxSim over token pairs → cross-encoder-ish quality
Precomputable ∴ usable at retrieval and rerank
Price: storage blows up (many vectors per chunk)

links.label: Multi Vector Embeddings — ColBERT & Late Interaction

questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: token-level vectors → MaxSim → precomputed → quality without joint pass

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q30: "ColBERT and late interaction — what does it keep from bi-encoders, what does it steal from cross-encoders, and what's the bill?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: It refuses to compress a document into one vector. What does it store instead, and what cheap operation replaces full cross-attention at query time?
points: ColBERT stores one vector per token, not one per document — encoding stays independent (kept from bi-encoders: precomputable, indexable), but scoring becomes MaxSim: each query token finds its best-matching document token, and those maxima sum.

What that steals from cross-encoders: token-level interaction — fine-grained matching without joint attention, so exact terms and specific phrases matter again instead of being averaged into a document soup.

The bill: index size explodes — hundreds of vectors per document instead of one — which is why real deployments quantize/pool aggressively and mostly use it as a reranking tier rather than the primary index.
Where it sits: quality and cost both land between bi- and cross-encoders — a middle rung for when the cross-encoder's latency doesn't fit but single-vector precision isn't enough.
Placement in one phrase: representation like a bi-encoder, interaction (late, cheap) like a cross-encoder.
drill.oneLiner: ColBERT keeps bi-encoder precomputability but stores a vector per token and scores with MaxSim — cross-encoder-flavored token matching at ANN-ish speed, paid for in index size.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q10: "Chunk size: what actually happens to retrieval and to generation as you turn that dial?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Two curves move in opposite directions — one belongs to the embedding, one to the LLM's context budget.
points: Small chunks → each vector is sharp → retrieval precision rises, but the retrieved fragment may lack enough context to answer, and you need more of them.

Large chunks → self-contained context, but the vector dilutes (recall the centroid argument) and each retrieved chunk drags irrelevant text into the prompt — noise the model must ignore, tokens you pay for.
Generation side: k × chunk-size is your context spend — bigger chunks at the same k means higher latency, higher cost, and more lost-in-the-middle risk.
There is no universal number: right size tracks the corpus's idea density (dense API docs vs discursive policy prose) — which is why it's a tuned hyperparameter against a golden set.
The escape hatch from the dilemma is decoupling — which is the next question.
drill.oneLiner: Chunk size trades embedding sharpness against answer completeness, and every extra token per chunk is multiplied by k in the prompt — it's a measured hyperparameter, not a constant you memorize.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q28: "Retrieve-many-rerank-few: how do you size each stage of the funnel, and what evidence drives the numbers?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Each stage has one job and one metric. Which stage is allowed to be sloppy, and in which direction?
points: Division of labor: first stage maximizes recall (it may be sloppy about precision — false positives are fine, false negatives are fatal); reranker restores precision; the LLM gets only what fits attention.

Stage-1 size (retrieve N): sweep recall@N on the golden set — set N at the knee where recall flattens. Below the knee you're starving the reranker; far above it you're paying rerank latency for nothing.
Stage-2 size (keep k): bounded by context budget and lost-in-the-middle — small, curated; validated by end-answer quality, not retrieval metrics.
Reranker cost model: latency scales linearly with N (one forward pass per candidate pair) — N is your latency lever; batch and parallelize, or use a lighter reranker tier if the budget is tight.
Also in this stage: dedup near-identical candidates before reranking (don't spend rerank budget scoring five copies) and diversity selection after.
The trap to name: tuning stage-1 on precision — its only job is to not lose the answer; precision is the next stage's job.
drill.oneLiner: Size the wide end where recall@N flattens on your eval set, size the narrow end by context budget, and remember stage one is graded only on not losing the answer — precision is what you pay the reranker for.

Three suspects left: ranking (buried at 40) · assembly (truncation, lost-in-middle, conflicts) · generation (ignores context, uses parametric memory)

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q31: "Your RAG answers are fluent but wrong, and retrieval logs look fine — where do you look first?"
drill.badge: Trending — the failure-attribution scenario; recurs on 2026 interview banks + production-RAG postmortem writeups (2025–26)
drill.hint: "Retrieval logs look fine" means similarity scores were high. Two very different suspects remain: what happened between retrieval and the prompt, and what the model did with the prompt.
points: First move: pull the trace for one bad answer and ask "was the correct answer text actually present in the final assembled prompt?" — that single check splits the search space in half.

If it wasn't there: retrieval "looked fine" but wasn't — high similarity ≠ relevant (near-miss chunks), or the right chunk was retrieved then lost in assembly: truncated by the token budget, deduped away, crowded out, or the index served a stale version of the document.

If it was there: a groundedness failure — the model ignored or contradicted its context (position effects from Q29, conflicting chunks where it picked the wrong one, or parametric knowledge overriding the document).

Instrument accordingly: per-stage tracing (query → rewritten query → candidates → reranked set → assembled prompt → answer) plus a faithfulness score per response — then this diagnosis is a dashboard filter, not an archaeology dig.
The senior framing: "retrieval metrics green + answers wrong" almost always means your metrics measure similarity, not sufficiency — the eval gap is itself a finding.
drill.oneLiner: I check whether the answer's evidence existed in the final assembled prompt — if not, it's a silent retrieval or assembly loss despite pretty similarity scores; if yes, it's a groundedness failure, and each has a completely different fix.
drill.followUp: "How do you catch this class before users do?" → Continuous faithfulness scoring on sampled production traffic with alerting (Q45).

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q35: "When do you promote retrieval from a fixed pipeline stage to a tool an agent calls in a loop — and what does that cost you?"
drill.badge: Trending — the 2026 shift: agentic RAG recurs across 2026 interview banks + GenAI JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Standard RAG is a special case of the agent version with exactly one mandatory retrieval. What query classes need the loop — and name the three bills that arrive with it.
points: The reframe interviewers now expect: pipeline RAG = exactly one mandatory retrieval, fixed order; agentic RAG = the model decides when to search, what to search, which source, and whether results suffice — retrieval becomes a tool among tools.

Promote when: multi-hop questions where hop N depends on hop N−1's answer, heterogeneous sources needing dynamic choice (SQL + docs + web), or queries needing a sufficiency judgment ("keep digging or answer?"). A fixed pipeline structurally can't do these.

The three bills: latency (serial tool-loop round trips vs one pass), cost (multiple model calls per query), and debuggability — a non-deterministic trajectory replaces a fixed pipeline, so failures need trace-level attribution and eval becomes trajectory eval, not stage eval.
Guardrails you must mention: loop budgets (max tool calls, token ceiling), graded fallback to single-shot on budget exhaustion, and per-step logging.
The honest architecture answer: most traffic doesn't need the loop — route (Q26/Adaptive): pipeline for the simple 80%, agent for the compound 20%.
drill.oneLiner: Promote retrieval to a tool when the query needs decisions between retrievals — dependent hops, source choice, sufficiency checks — and accept that you're buying adaptivity with latency, cost, and a much harder debugging story, so route only the hard queries into the loop.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q36: "'Summarize the main themes across our whole knowledge base.' Why does vanilla RAG fail this, and what actually handles it?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Top-k retrieval answers local questions. This question is global. What two architectures pre-compute the global view at ingestion time?
points: Why it fails structurally: top-k similarity fetches the k most similar fragments — but a "themes" query isn't similar to any particular chunk; the answer is a property of the whole corpus, and no k covers it. This is a query-class mismatch, not a tuning problem.

GraphRAG: at ingestion, extract entities/relations into a knowledge graph, cluster into communities, and pre-write community summaries — global questions are answered over summaries (map-reduce style), local questions can traverse relationships vectors can't express ("everything connected to X").

RAPTOR: recursively cluster chunks and summarize each cluster, building a tree of abstraction levels — retrieval can then hit leaves for detail questions and upper nodes for thematic ones, within one index.

Both shift heavy cost to ingestion (LLM extraction/summarization over the corpus, plus keeping graph/tree fresh as documents change) — that's the bill for answering global queries at interactive speed.
Deployment reality: hybrid — route global/relational queries to graph or tree, keep vanilla vector RAG for the local factoid majority.
drill.oneLiner: Theme questions are global and top-k is local by construction — GraphRAG's community summaries and RAPTOR's summary tree pre-compute the global views at ingestion, and a router sends each query to the level it actually needs.

questions.text: Semantic chunking vs recursive splitting — worth the cost?
points: Recursive = split on separators (¶ → sentence → char) — cheap, predictable, strong baseline
Semantic = embed sentences, cut at similarity troughs — better boundaries, embed cost at ingest
Structure-aware beats both when the doc has real structure (headings, tables)
Measure recall@k before paying for semantic
questions.badge: Trending — recurs across 2026 RAG interview banks + Medium/TDS production-RAG posts (2025–26)
questions.flow: has structure? → structure-aware · else recursive baseline · semantic only if measured
questions.trap: assuming semantic chunking is strictly better

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q9: "Fixed, recursive, structure-aware, semantic, propositional — how do you actually pick a chunking strategy?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs across 2026 RAG interview banks + Medium/TDS production-RAG posts (2025–26)
drill.hint: Rank them by how much document structure they respect versus what they cost — and name the default that wins most production bake-offs.
points: Fixed-size: dumb but predictable — cuts mid-sentence, mid-thought. Baseline only.
Recursive splitting: tries separators in order (paragraph → sentence → word) to respect natural boundaries within a size cap — the production default; cheap and rarely embarrassing.
Structure-aware: splits on headings/sections from layout-aware parsing — best when documents have reliable structure (docs sites, contracts, manuals); inherits parsing quality.
Semantic chunking: embeds sentences and cuts where similarity drops — respects topic shifts, costs embedding calls at ingest, and its wins over recursive are corpus-dependent — measure, don't assume.
Propositional / contextual / late chunking: decompose into atomic facts or enrich each chunk with LLM-generated context — highest quality, highest ingest cost; justify with eval numbers, not vibes.
The senior frame: chunking is an eval-driven decision — pick recursive, build the golden set, then let recall@k justify anything fancier.
drill.oneLiner: Default to recursive splitting, upgrade to structure-aware when documents have real structure, and only pay for semantic or propositional chunking when your eval set proves the lift.
drill.followUp: "What about overlap?" → Small overlap insures against boundary cuts; it's a patch, not a strategy — too much bloats the index with near-duplicates.

questions.text: How do you choose an embedding model?
points: Your data, not MTEB — leaderboards are proxies; build a golden set and measure recall@k
Axes: dimension (storage/RAM) · max seq length · asymmetric-trained? · domain fit · license/hosting
Matryoshka dims → truncate for cheap ANN, full dim for rerank
Quantized (int8/binary) → big RAM win, small recall cost
Switching cost = full reindex → treat as a versioned decision
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: golden set → measure on your corpus → then weigh dim / seq len / hosting

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q13: "How do you choose an embedding model for a domain-heavy corpus — and what does a leaderboard rank not tell you?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: The leaderboard measured someone else's corpus. What's the only evaluation that counts, and what non-quality axes constrain the choice?
points: Benchmarks like MTEB average over generic tasks and public datasets — a top rank doesn't transfer to legal/medical/internal jargon, and popular benchmarks suffer contamination/overfitting pressure. Use them to shortlist, never to decide.
The deciding eval: your own golden set — recall@k / nDCG on your corpus with your query style. Shortlist three models, run the bake-off.

Non-quality axes that eliminate candidates first: dimensionality (index RAM and cost scale with it), max input length, latency/throughput, hosted-API vs self-hosted (data residency, cost per million tokens), license.
Practical trap to name: switching models later means re-embedding the entire corpus (Q44) — model choice is a longer commitment than it looks.

If no general model clears the bar on domain vocabulary: fine-tune the embedder on mined (query, relevant-passage) pairs — cheaper than people assume and often the biggest single retrieval lift on niche corpora.
drill.oneLiner: Shortlist from the leaderboard, decide on your own golden set — and remember dimensionality, input length, hosting, and the re-embedding lock-in are as binding as quality.
drill.followUp: "Where do fine-tuning pairs come from?" → Mined from logs (clicked/cited chunks) or synthetically generated questions per chunk, human-spot-checked.

questions.text: Query rewriting vs multi-query vs decomposition — which when?

Multi-query — one intent, several phrasings → union → recall insurance
Decomposition — genuinely multi-part question → sub-questions → answer each
Step-back — too-specific query → ask the general question first
Each costs an LLM call + latency; decomposition costs N retrievals

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q23: "A question needs facts from three different documents, and single-shot retrieval keeps missing at least one. What are your options?"
drill.badge: Evergreen — the multi-hop question.
drill.hint: One query embedding is one point in space — it can't be near three different neighborhoods at once. How do you get more points?
points: Root cause: a single query embedding is one point — a compound question ("compare X's policy with Y's, considering Z") averages into a mush that sits near none of the three targets.
Multi-query retrieval: LLM generates several rephrasings, retrieve for each in parallel, union/RRF the pools — cheap, parallel, attacks phrasing luck.

Sub-question decomposition: split into genuinely different questions ("What is X's policy?", "What is Y's?"), retrieve per sub-question, answer compositionally — the right tool when the information needs differ, not just the phrasing.

Iterative/recursive retrieval: retrieve → read → let the model discover what's still missing → retrieve again — required when hop 2 depends on hop 1's answer (true multi-hop); costs a serial LLM round-trip per hop.

Escalation path to say: multi-query (parallel, cheap) → decomposition (parallel, structured) → iterative (serial, expensive) → full agentic loop (Q35) — pay for exactly as much adaptivity as the question class needs.
drill.oneLiner: One embedding can't stand near three answers — fan out with multi-query, decompose when the information needs differ, and go iterative only when the next hop depends on the last answer.

questions.text: Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE — what does each fix?

CRAG — grade retrieved docs; on bad grade, fall back (web search / rewrite)
FLARE — retrieve mid-generation when the model's confidence drops
Shared idea: retrieval becomes conditional, not a fixed first step
All add latency and non-determinism → need caps

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q34: "Self-RAG, Corrective RAG, Adaptive RAG — what specific failure of the naive loop does each one patch?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Map each to one naive-RAG sin: retrieving when you shouldn't, trusting junk you retrieved, and spending the same effort on every query.
points: The shared move: all three add reflection/grading steps to a loop that previously trusted itself blindly — "modular RAG" is naive RAG plus judgment at the joints.

Self-RAG patches unconditional retrieval and unconditional trust: the model decides whether to retrieve, critiques retrieved passages for relevance, and critiques its own draft for support before answering.

Corrective RAG (CRAG) patches garbage-in, garbage-through: a lightweight grader scores retrieved docs; good → proceed, ambiguous → refine/filter, bad → fall back (e.g., web search or a different index) instead of generating from junk.

Adaptive RAG patches one-size-fits-all cost: classify query complexity first — simple factoid gets single-shot retrieval or no retrieval; multi-hop gets the iterative machinery — spend proportional to difficulty.

The trade-off to volunteer: every added grade/critique step is another LLM call in the latency path and another component to evaluate — these patterns are graded rollouts, not defaults. (FLARE extends the family: retrieve mid-generation when confidence dips.)
drill.oneLiner: Self-RAG makes retrieval and trust conditional, CRAG grades the evidence and falls back instead of generating from junk, Adaptive RAG spends retrieval effort proportional to query complexity — each one bolts judgment onto a joint naive RAG left blind.

questions.text: How do you set top-k?
points: Retrieval k and generation k are different numbers — over-retrieve, send few
Raise retrieval k until recall@k plateaus on the golden set
Generation k bounded by context budget + lost-in-middle + cost per token
Reranker lets generation k shrink → cheaper and more accurate
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: retrieve wide to plateau → rerank → send the few that survive
questions.trap: one k for both stages

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q22: "How do you set top-k — and what actually goes wrong at k too small and k too large?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: One direction fails loudly, the other fails expensively and quietly. And what post-processing step changes the k calculus entirely?
points: k too small → the answer chunk simply isn't in the pool: hard recall failure no downstream stage can fix.
k too large → context stuffed with near-misses: noise dilutes attention (lost-in-the-middle), latency and token cost climb, and paradoxically answer quality can drop as k rises — more is not better.

k is not one number: it splits into k-retrieve (generous, cheap — feed the reranker) and k-final (small, curated — feed the LLM). The retrieve-many-rerank-few funnel (Q28) dissolves most of the k agonizing.

Refinements to name: similarity-score floors (drop garbage even inside top-k — with the caveat that raw cosine thresholds are corpus-relative), and MMR to trade pure relevance for diversity when top-k returns five copies of the same paragraph.
How you actually set it: sweep k on the golden set, watch recall@k flatten — the knee of that curve is your k-retrieve; token budget sets k-final.
drill.oneLiner: Small k fails hard on recall, large k fails soft on noise and cost — so split it: retrieve generously for the reranker, hand the model a curated few, and let the recall@k curve on your eval set place the knee.

questions.badge: Evergreen — the ANN-filter problem; most candidates have never thought about it.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q18: "You add a tenant filter to the query and recall craters for small tenants. What's happening inside the index?"
drill.badge: Evergreen — the ANN-filter problem; most candidates have never thought about it.
drill.hint: The index was built over all vectors, but you only want a sliver. What happens if you filter after the walk — and what happens to the graph walk if you filter during it?
points: Post-filtering: ANN returns top-k over the whole space, then the filter drops non-matching results — for a tenant owning 0.1% of vectors, most of the k evaporates and you return three results or none. That's the crater.

Pre-filtering / filter-aware search: constrain the search itself — but naively restricting an HNSW walk to allowed nodes fragments the graph's connectivity, so quality degrades differently. Modern engines do filter-aware traversal (keep walking through disallowed nodes, only collect allowed ones) to mitigate.

Third option: partitioning — a namespace/index per tenant makes the filter structural. Perfect isolation, but thousands of tiny indexes bring their own management cost (and tiny partitions lose ANN's economies).
Selectivity is the decision variable: highly selective filter → partition or pre-filter; mildly selective → post-filter with oversampling (fetch k × margin, then filter).
This is also a security question: for tenant isolation, filtering is enforcement — post-filter bugs become data leaks (ties into Q43).
drill.oneLiner: That's the ANN-filter problem — post-filtering starves selective queries and naive pre-filtering breaks graph connectivity, so you choose by selectivity: oversample-and-filter, filter-aware traversal, or partition per tenant.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q7: "Your corpus changes daily — wiki edits, deletions, new uploads. Design the sync so the index never serves stale or deleted content."
drill.badge: Evergreen — the question that separates demo-builders from system-owners.
drill.hint: Three sub-problems: how you detect change, how you apply it to derived chunks, and what "deleted" must mean all the way down.
points: Detection: event-driven (webhooks/CDC from the source system) beats polling; polling with content hashes per document is the fallback. Never re-ingest the world on a timer as the primary strategy.

The unit of update is the document, not the chunk: on change, delete all chunks derived from the old version and insert the new ones — diffing chunks in place drifts. That requires a stable doc-id → chunk-ids mapping in metadata.
Deletions are the compliance case: a tombstone must propagate to every derived artifact — chunks, vectors, caches, and any semantic answer cache that memorized the old content.
Consistency: updates aren't atomic across chunks — accept brief staleness but make it bounded and monitored (indexing lag as a first-class metric).
Versioning guard: an in-flight query can see mixed old/new chunks; version-stamp chunks and prefer filtering to the latest doc version at query time.
drill.oneLiner: Detect via events or content hashes, re-derive at document granularity with a doc-to-chunks mapping, and treat deletion as a tombstone that must chase the content through vectors and caches — with indexing lag monitored as an SLO.
drill.followUp: "What's your staleness SLO and who owns it?" → Depends on domain — minutes for support KB, hours for policy docs; the ingestion pipeline owns it.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q42: "Your product owner demands p95 under two seconds end-to-end. Break down where the time goes in a RAG request and what you cut first."
drill.badge: Trending — latency-budget breakdowns recur on production-RAG writeups + GenAI JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Walk the request: embed → search → rerank → assemble → generate. One stage dwarfs the rest — so where do the real savings come from, and which cache pays off at each stage?
points: Budget walk, and say the shape: query embedding (one small model call) → ANN search (typically milliseconds — rarely the villain) → rerank (scales linearly with candidate count N) → assembly (negligible) → generation, which dominates — and within it, time-to-first-token plus output length are what the user feels. Any LLM steps you added (rewriter, router, judge) each stack a full round-trip.

Cut order: stream tokens (perceived latency collapses even if total time doesn't) → shrink the prompt (fewer/tighter chunks — compression from Q29 is also a latency tool) and cap output length → trim reranker N or use a lighter reranker tier → run rewriter/router on small fast models or skip them for simple queries (adaptive routing as a latency lever).

Caching ladder: embedding cache (repeated queries skip the encoder) → retrieval cache (query → chunk-IDs) → semantic answer cache (similar-enough question → stored answer; the big win on FAQ-heavy traffic, with a staleness/invalidation story tied to Q7) → provider prompt caching (stable system prompt + instructions as a cached prefix, volatile chunks after — order the prompt so the cacheable part comes first).
Parallelize what's parallel: dense + BM25 legs concurrently, multi-query fan-out concurrently — the serial spine should be as short as possible.
Close like an architect: publish a per-stage latency budget and trace against it (Q45's observability) — "under 2s" is a contract you allocate, not a hope.
drill.oneLiner: Generation dominates, so stream first and shrink the prompt second, keep the ANN and reranker legs lean and parallel, then climb the caching ladder from embeddings to semantic answers to provider prompt-prefix caching — against an explicit per-stage budget.
drill.followUp: "Semantic cache hit criteria?" → Similarity threshold plus matching filters/tenant and index version — a cross-tenant or stale-version cache hit is a correctness bug, not a win.

points: Every existing vector is now incomparable — no partial migration, no mixed index
Blue/green: build new index in parallel → shadow queries → compare recall@k on golden set → cut over → keep old for rollback
Dimension change → storage/RAM re-plan
Version-stamp the index; queries must never straddle two embedding spaces

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q44: "You want to swap the embedding model. What else must change with it — and how do you roll it out with zero downtime?"
drill.badge: Evergreen — the question that reveals whether someone has operated RAG, not just built it.
drill.hint: Two different models produce vectors in two unrelated spaces. What does that force about the index — and what's the deployment pattern borrowed from every risky migration ever?
points: The physics: two embedding models define incompatible vector spaces — old document vectors and new query vectors are meaningless to compare. There is no partial swap: the entire corpus re-embeds, full stop. Budget that (tokens × corpus size) before agreeing to the change.

The coupling: embedder, chunking config, index parameters, similarity thresholds, and prompts version together as one system — a new embedder shifts the score distribution, so every hardcoded similarity floor (abstention gates from Q32, cache hit thresholds from Q42) silently mis-calibrates. Version the bundle, not the model.

Rollout: build a shadow index with the new model via the offline pipeline (the ingestion/serving separation is what makes this possible at all) → run the golden set against both (Q41) → shadow-serve a slice of real traffic comparing outputs → cut over by config flip, keep the old index warm for instant rollback.
During transition: dual-write new/changed documents to both indexes, or freeze ingestion for the window — otherwise the shadow index drifts while you evaluate it.
Same playbook covers the quieter cousin: embedding drift — the model didn't change but the corpus/query language did; re-embedding strategy is a scheduled decision, not an emergency.
drill.oneLiner: A new embedder is a new vector space — full re-embed into a shadow index, re-tune every similarity threshold as part of a versioned bundle, prove it on the golden set and shadow traffic, then flip with the old index warm for rollback.
drill.followUp: "What if the corpus is too big to re-embed affordably?" → That cost was part of choosing the model (Q13) — mitigate with Matryoshka/quantization tiers, or conclude the swap isn't worth the lift.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q29: "The right chunk is in the prompt — position 7 of 15 — and the model still ignores it. Diagnose and fix."
drill.badge: Evergreen — retrieval succeeded; assembly failed.
drill.hint: Where in a long context does model attention actually land — and what are the two levers: where you put the chunk, and how much competition it faces?
points: Name the phenomenon: lost in the middle — models attend most reliably to the beginning and end of the context; mid-positions get measurably less use. Retrieval metrics are green, the answer is wrong, and the bug is in prompt assembly.
Lever 1 — reordering: place the strongest chunks at the edges (best first, second-best last, weakest buried in the middle) — a zero-cost assembly change.

Lever 2 — less competition: 15 chunks is likely too many — compress (strip irrelevant sentences, contextual compression) and dedup near-identical chunks that crowd attention without adding information.
Also check the boring causes first: chunk truncated by the token budget, separators/formatting mangling chunk boundaries, or the system prompt instructing the model in ways that fight the context.
Detection signal: your groundedness eval passes when the same chunk is placed first but fails at position 7 — position sensitivity is measurable, so measure it.
drill.oneLiner: Retrieval delivered and assembly buried it — that's lost in the middle; reorder so the best evidence sits at the context edges, then shrink the competition with compression and dedup instead of shipping fifteen chunks.

questions.flow: isolation model → principal-derived filter inside ANN → ACL recheck → canary test

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q43: "Multi-tenant RAG where tenant A must never see tenant B's chunks — where does enforcement live, and why isn't the prompt enough?"
drill.badge: Trending — RAG security/ACL questions recur on 2026 interview banks + enterprise GenAI JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: The model is the least trustworthy component in the system. Which stage is the last one where a deterministic system can still say no — and don't forget the caches.
points: The principle first: enforcement lives at retrieval, not generation — "please only use tenant A's documents" is a suggestion to a stochastic model; a chunk that enters the prompt must be assumed leakable. The filter must be a deterministic system boundary.

Mechanics: every chunk carries tenant/ACL metadata stamped at ingestion; query-time filtering is server-side and mandatory (derived from the authenticated session, never from model- or client-supplied parameters). Namespace/partition-per-tenant makes isolation structural — and recall the ANN-filter recall problem (Q18) as the engineering cost of the filtered approach.

The leak paths people forget: caches (semantic answer cache must be tenant-scoped or it will serve A's answer to B), logs and traces containing chunks, eval datasets sampled from production, and stale ACLs — permission revocation must propagate to the index like deletion in Q7.

Document-level ACLs within a tenant are the harder version: user-level permission checks at query time against groups/roles — pre-filter by ACL metadata, and re-check at assembly if permissions are volatile.

Adjacent threat to volunteer: indirect prompt injection — retrieved content itself carrying instructions ("ignore previous instructions…") — meaning the index is an attack surface: sanitize/ingest-scan, treat retrieved text as data not instructions in prompt framing, and never give the generation step more authority than the retrieving user has.
drill.oneLiner: Tenant isolation is enforced at retrieval by server-side ACL filters and per-tenant namespaces — never by the prompt — and the same rigor must chase the data into caches, logs, and revocations, while retrieved content itself is treated as untrusted input.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q37: "Why is RAG evaluation two separate problems — and what goes wrong for teams that only evaluate end-to-end?"
drill.badge: Evergreen — the section opener; everything in this section hangs off it.
drill.hint: Two components, two different questions, two different ground truths. And end-to-end-only teams can see that it's broken but never what…
points: The split: retrieval quality ("did the right chunks come back?" — graded against labeled relevant chunks, with rank-aware metrics) and generation quality ("given those chunks, was the answer faithful and useful?" — graded against the context and the question). Different questions, different ground truth, different metrics.
End-to-end-only failure: the score drops and you can't attribute — was it chunking, the embedder, k, assembly, or the prompt? Every debugging session starts from zero.

Worse: end-to-end can mask compensation — a strong LLM papering over mediocre retrieval from its parametric knowledge looks fine until the corpus diverges from the model's training data, then fails silently.
Component eval also isolates changes: swap the reranker and check retrieval metrics moved without touching the generation config — that's how you A/B one stage at a time (Q41).
Keep end-to-end too — components can each pass while the composition fails; you need both layers, with component metrics for attribution and end-to-end for truth.
drill.oneLiner: Retrieval and generation have different ground truths, so grade them separately — end-to-end-only eval tells you that it broke but never where, and it lets a strong model quietly compensate for a weak retriever until the day it can't.

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q25: "Mid-conversation the user asks, 'and what about the second option?' Retrieval returns junk. Fix the pipeline."
drill.badge: Evergreen — every chat-over-docs product hits this in week one.
drill.hint: The embedder sees exactly the string you give it. What does "the second option" embed as, and what step is missing before retrieval?
points: Root cause: the message is anaphoric — "the second one", "what about pricing?", "does it?" are meaningless without history, and the embedder sees only the literal string. Retrieval on it is retrieval on noise.

The fix is a query contextualization step: an LLM rewrites the turn into a standalone question using conversation history ("what are the trade-offs of option B — the managed vector DB?"), and that string goes to retrieval.
What not to do: embed the whole conversation (drowns the current intent in history) or concatenate the last N turns (drags in stale topics after a subject change).

Engineering notes: the rewriter is a small/fast model — it's on every turn's latency path; log the rewritten query, because now retrieval failures split into rewrite failures vs retrieval failures and you must attribute correctly.
Also decide when not to retrieve: "thanks, that's clear!" needs no retrieval — a lightweight gate saves latency and noise.
drill.oneLiner: Follow-ups are anaphora — condense the turn plus history into a standalone query before embedding, log that rewritten query for debugging, and gate turns that don't need retrieval at all.

Dense is short and fully populated — typically 384–3072 dims, every value meaningful
Storage flips the intuition: sparse is stored as term→weight pairs, so it's often smaller on disk

This is a screen filter — answer it in one line, then move to why you'd fuse both

points: Abstention is a feature. A grader on retrieved context decides answer / clarify / refuse
Trigger on: no chunk over the relevance bar · contradictory sources (#34) · out-of-scope query · low-confidence generation
Refusal must be useful — say what's missing, offer the nearest scoped question, don't just say "I don't know"
Pairs with citation: every claim traceable, or the answer isn't shippable
Tune the threshold deliberately — over-refusal reads as broken, under-refusal as lying

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_rag Q32: "How do you build a RAG system that says 'I don't know' — and what should it do when two retrieved sources disagree?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Prompting "say IDK if unsure" is the naive layer. What pipeline signals tell you the context can't support an answer — before and after generation?
points: Why it matters: an ungrounded "best guess" in a RAG product is worse than no answer — users treat retrieved-and-cited output as authoritative.

Abstention layers, weakest to strongest: prompt instruction ("answer only from context") → pre-generation gate: if reranker/relevance scores for all candidates are below a floor, short-circuit to "not found in the knowledge base" without calling the LLM → post-generation check: verify the draft is supported by the context (a groundedness scorer), suppress or hedge if not.
The pre-generation gate is the underrated one — it saves the generation cost and is more reliable than asking the model to self-assess.
Conflicting sources: first try to resolve by metadata — recency, authority tier, version (the policy doc beats the old email thread); encode that priority in assembly order and prompt framing.

If genuinely unresolvable: surface the conflict — "source A says X (2026), source B says Y (2023)" with citations — never silently average, and log conflicts as a data-quality signal for the corpus owners.
Tune the abstention threshold on your eval set: over-abstention quietly kills product trust just like hallucination does — it's a precision/recall trade on answering itself.
drill.oneLiner: Abstention is a pipeline property, not a prompt line — gate on retrieval confidence before generating, verify groundedness after, and when sources conflict, resolve by recency and authority or surface the disagreement with citations rather than averaging it away.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q1 · S1 Foundations) "What problem does RAG actually solve that a bigger prompt or a better model doesn't? You have 30 seconds.
points: The model's parametric knowledge is frozen at training time and inscrutable — you can't update it, can't cite it, can't permission it.
RAG attaches non-parametric memory at inference: a store you can update tonight, inspect per-answer, and gate per-user.
The four wins to name: freshness, provenance/citations, access control, and grounding on private data the model never saw.
Say the caveat: RAG reduces hallucination by grounding, it doesn't eliminate it — the model can still contradict its context.
Bonus signal: it also decouples knowledge cost from model cost — updating a document is cheap; retraining is not.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the opener; the trap is answering only "hallucinations".
questions.oneLiner: RAG bolts a swappable, inspectable knowledge store onto a frozen model — freshness, provenance, and permissioning that prompting alone can't retrofit.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q4 · S1 Foundations) "Give me three situations where you'd talk a team out of building RAG.
points: Reasoning/skill tasks, not knowledge tasks — math, code transforms, general writing: there's nothing to retrieve; RAG adds latency and a new failure surface.
Tiny stable corpus — if the whole thing fits comfortably in context and rarely changes, a system prompt or prompt-cached context beats an index.
Aggregate/global questions over the corpus ("what are the main themes?") — top-k retrieval structurally can't see the whole; you need summarization trees or GraphRAG, not vanilla RAG.
Structured data with exact-answer semantics — "revenue last quarter by region" is a SQL query, not a similarity search; Text-to-SQL beats embedding tables.
The meta-point: RAG is an architecture with real operational cost (ingestion, index, eval, drift) — you buy it when the knowledge properties demand it.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q5 · S2 Ingestion & Parsing) "Your PDF ingestion 'works,' but every question about a table gets a confidently wrong answer. What happened upstream?
points: Naive PDF extraction linearizes by position, not meaning: multi-column pages interleave, tables flatten into word soup, headers/footers pollute every page, reading order breaks.

A flattened table loses row-column association — the embedding still "looks" relevant (right entities, right numbers), so retrieval logs look fine while the cell relationships are gone. That's why the answer is confidently wrong.

Fixes, cheap to expensive: layout-aware parsers that emit structured table output (HTML/markdown) → table-specific extraction and per-table chunks → table summaries embedded for retrieval with raw table returned for generation.
For scanned or visually complex docs: OCR quality gates, or vision-model parsing of page images.
Say the principle: retrieval quality is capped by parsing quality — no downstream trick recovers structure destroyed at ingestion.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the dirty secret of every enterprise RAG deployment.
questions.oneLiner: The extractor flattened the table — the chunk still embeds as 'relevant' but the row-column structure is gone, so retrieval passes and generation fabricates; fix it at parse time with structure-preserving extraction.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q6 · S2 Ingestion & Parsing) "When does layout-aware parsing earn its cost over plain text extraction?
points: Plain extraction is fine for linear prose (articles, transcripts, plain reports). Layout parsing earns its cost when structure carries semantics: headings hierarchy, tables, forms, multi-column, figures with captions.
What layout-aware parsing buys: correct reading order, section hierarchy you can chunk on, tables as tables, and metadata (section titles, page numbers) that powers filtering and citations later.
Multimodal documents (charts, diagrams, screenshots): text extraction returns nothing useful — you need vision-model description or multimodal embedding for those regions.
Cost axis: layout/vision parsing is orders slower and pricier per page — so route by document class, don't run the expensive path on everything.
Downstream coupling: structure-aware chunking (Section 3) is only possible if parsing preserved the structure — this decision cascades.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Layout parsing pays off exactly when meaning lives in structure — tables, hierarchies, columns, figures — and its output is what makes structure-aware chunking and citations possible downstream.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q8 · S3 Chunking) "Why chunk at all — why not embed each document whole?
points: An embedding is a fixed-size vector: embed a whole document and every topic in it gets averaged into one point — the vector becomes a blurry centroid that matches nothing sharply. Dilution, not truncation, is the core argument.
Second reason: retrieval granularity — you want to hand the LLM the relevant passage, not 40 pages, for cost, latency, and attention.
Third: embedding models have their own input token limits — long docs get silently truncated, so tail content becomes unretrievable.
The tension chunking manages: chunks small enough to embed one idea sharply, large enough to be answerable context — the whole of Section 3 is negotiating that.
questions.badge: Evergreen — warm-up; the answer is about embeddings, not context windows.
questions.oneLiner: A whole-document embedding averages every topic into one blurry vector — chunking exists so each vector means one thing sharply and the LLM receives passages, not books.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q12 · S4 Embeddings) "What is an embedding, mechanically — and why is cosine similarity between two of them a meaningful number?
points: An embedding is a learned map from text to a fixed-dimension vector where the training objective (typically contrastive: pull related pairs together, push unrelated apart) makes geometric closeness track semantic relatedness.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors — meaningful only because training shaped the space that way; it's a property of the model, not of math.
With normalized vectors, cosine, dot product, and Euclidean ranking coincide — say this and you've covered the distance-metric question; use the metric the model was trained with.
"Semantic" means the model's notion of similarity from its training distribution — which is exactly why domain mismatch (Q13) degrades retrieval.
Dimensions are not interpretable features; only the geometry as a whole carries meaning.
questions.badge: Evergreen — definition under pressure; hand-waving here ends the interview early.
questions.oneLiner: An embedding is a contrastively-trained projection where the training objective made angle track relatedness — cosine similarity is meaningful because the model was optimized to make it so, not because geometry is magic.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q15 · S4 Embeddings) "Your vector storage and memory bill is the biggest line item. Walk me through shrinking it without gutting recall.
points: Vector footprint = count × dimensions × bytes-per-dimension. You can attack all three.

Matryoshka embeddings: trained so meaning concentrates in the leading dimensions — truncate to a prefix for a large storage cut with modest quality loss; pick the cut by re-running your eval at each size.
Quantization: float32 → int8 (4× smaller, minor loss) → binary (32× smaller, real loss) — Hamming distance on binary vectors is extremely fast.

The pattern that makes aggressive compression safe: coarse search on compressed vectors, then rescore the shortlist with full-precision vectors kept on cheaper storage — recall recovered, RAM bill cut.
Index-level equivalent is product quantization (PQ) inside IVF-family indexes — same idea, applied by the index rather than at the embedding layer.
Don't skip the boring lever: do fewer/smaller chunks and dedup near-identical content — count is the first multiplier.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the 2025–26 cost-engineering staple.
questions.oneLiner: Cut dimensions with Matryoshka truncation, cut bytes with int8 or binary quantization, and protect recall by rescoring a compressed-search shortlist against full-precision vectors.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q20 · S6 Retrieval) "What does dense bi-encoder retrieval do well — and name two query classes where it reliably loses to keyword search.
points: Bi-encoder dense retrieval: query and passages embedded independently, similarity = one vector comparison — that independence is what makes pre-computing an index possible and search fast.
Its strength: vocabulary mismatch — "How do I get my money back?" finds the refund policy with zero shared words; synonyms, paraphrase, cross-lingual.

Loses reliably on: exact identifiers — error codes, SKUs, function names, version strings ("v2.3.1"), people/product names — rare tokens the embedding smooths over; and out-of-distribution jargon the encoder never learned, which lands nowhere useful in the space.
Also weak on: negation and fine-grained distinctions — "not compatible" and "compatible" embed uncomfortably close.
This asymmetry of failure modes — dense fails on precision-of-token, sparse fails on paraphrase — is the entire argument for hybrid (next question).

questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Dense retrieval matches meaning, not tokens — brilliant on paraphrase, unreliable on exact identifiers and unseen jargon, which is precisely where BM25 is untouchable.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q26 · S7 Query Transformation & Routing) "You have a SQL warehouse, a document index, and a web search tool behind one chat box. Design the routing layer — and defend semantic routing vs LLM routing.
points: The router's job: classify each query to a datasource/tool (metrics question → Text-to-SQL; policy question → doc index; current events → web) — sending a SQL-shaped question to the vector index is a structural failure no retriever fixes.

Semantic routing: embed the query, compare against embedded route descriptions/exemplars — single embedding call, milliseconds, cheap, deterministic-ish; weak on compound or genuinely ambiguous queries.
LLM routing: a model reads the query and picks (with reasoning) — handles ambiguity, multi-route fan-out, and "needs both" cases; costs a model call in latency and money on every query.

Sane architecture: semantic router first with a confidence threshold; below threshold, escalate to the LLM router — fast path for the 80%, smart path for the hard 20%. Fan out to multiple routes when confidence ties.
Operational must: routing decisions are logged and evaluated like retrieval — a misroute is a retrieval failure that happened one stage earlier; build a routed-query eval slice.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q33 · S9 Generation & Augmentation) "Citations in RAG answers: how do you make them load-bearing rather than decorative?
points: The failure mode to name up front: hallucinated citations — the model emits a marker pointing at a chunk that doesn't support the sentence. A wrong citation is worse than none: it manufactures false confidence.

Mechanics: assign each retrieved chunk a stable ID in the prompt, instruct sentence-level attribution to those IDs, and prefer structured output (claims with source-ID arrays) over free-text markers so citations are machine-checkable.

Make them load-bearing with a verification pass: for each claim-citation pair, check the cited chunk actually entails the claim (an NLI-style or LLM check) — drop or flag the ones that fail. Citation precision is a metric, not a garnish.
UX side: citations must resolve to something a human can open — document, section, page — which is why metadata captured at ingestion (Q6) is what makes citation possible at all.
Streaming wrinkle: token-by-token streaming and post-hoc citation verification fight each other — verify per-sentence or accept flagging-after-render.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Give chunks stable IDs, demand structured claim-to-source attribution, then verify entailment per citation — a citation that isn't checked is decoration, and a wrong one is worse than none.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q38 · S11 Evaluation) "Recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG, hit rate — which metric answers which question about your retriever?
points: Recall@k — "of all relevant chunks, what fraction landed in the top k?" — the RAG workhorse: it directly answers "is the evidence in the pool I hand to the reranker/LLM?" Sets stage-1 k (Q28).
Precision@k — "what fraction of the top k is relevant?" — the context-noise metric; matters because irrelevant chunks cost tokens and attention.
Hit rate@k — binary "did at least one relevant chunk appear?" — coarse but honest for single-answer factoid workloads.
MRR — average of 1/rank of the first relevant result — right when one good chunk suffices and position matters; blind to everything after the first hit.

nDCG — rank-aware with graded relevance (highly vs partially relevant), discounted by position, normalized against the ideal ordering — the fairest single number when relevance isn't binary; the standard for judging rerankers.
The calibration point: order-blind metrics (recall/precision@k) are fine before a reranker; rank-aware ones (MRR/nDCG) are what prove the reranker earns its latency.

questions.oneLiner: Recall@k asks whether the evidence made the pool, precision@k asks how much junk came with it, MRR cares only where the first hit landed, and nDCG grades the whole ordering — pick per pipeline stage, not by habit.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q39 · S11 Evaluation) "Walk me through the RAG triad — and how does a framework like RAGAS actually compute faithfulness under the hood?
points: The triad covers the three edges: context relevance (question ↔ retrieved context: did we fetch the right stuff?), groundedness/faithfulness (context ↔ answer: is every claim supported?), answer relevance (answer ↔ question: did we address what was asked?). One edge failing tells you which component to open.
Why three: an answer can be fully grounded in irrelevant context, or relevant-and-hallucinated, or faithful-but-off-topic — a single score hides which sin occurred.

Faithfulness in RAGAS, mechanically: an LLM decomposes the answer into atomic claims, then checks each claim for support against the retrieved context; faithfulness = supported claims / total claims. It's automated NLI-by-LLM, not string matching.
Flagship property: several of these need no gold answer — they judge internal consistency of question/context/answer, which is what makes continuous production scoring possible (Q45).

The caveat that earns senior credit: these are LLM-judged metrics — they inherit judge biases and cost, so calibrate against a human-labeled slice before trusting absolute values (next question); treat them as regression detectors, not truth.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q40 · S11 Evaluation) "Your LLM-as-judge scores look great. Why don't you trust them yet?
points: The known biases, rapid-fire: position bias (favors the first answer in pairwise comparisons — mitigate by swapping order and averaging), verbosity bias (longer reads as better), self-preference (favors outputs of its own model family), style-over-substance (fluent-but-wrong scores well — exactly the RAG failure mode you care most about).
Plus mechanical fragility: score distributions shift with the rubric wording, scale, and judge model/version — a 4.2 is not comparable across setups, so absolute numbers mean little.
The trust procedure: calibrate against a human-labeled slice — measure judge-human agreement (and judge-judge stability) before believing anything; re-calibrate when you change judge model or prompt.

Design mitigations: pairwise comparison over absolute scoring, tight rubrics with anchored examples per grade, forcing reasoning before verdict, a judge model different from the generator, ensembling on high-stakes evals.
The bottom line stance: judges are scalable regression detectors — superb at "did this change make things worse on 500 examples overnight?", never a substitute for ground truth on absolute quality.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q41 · S11 Evaluation) "New domain, zero labeled data. Build me a golden set I can trust — then use it to judge a chunking change.
points: Bootstrap: synthetic Q&A generation — sample chunks, have an LLM write questions each chunk answers; you get (question, gold-chunk, reference-answer) triples with retrieval labels for free.

Trust ingredient 1 — human curation: synthetic questions skew easy, chunk-phrased, and single-hop; filter unanswerable/trivial ones and rewrite toward how users actually ask. Trust ingredient 2 — real distribution: mine production queries (or pilot logs) so the set reflects actual intents, including the messy, ambiguous, multi-hop ones synthesis undersamples.

Structure it: stratify by query class (factoid / multi-hop / table / no-answer) and report per-slice — aggregates hide exactly the slice your change broke. Include unanswerable questions to measure abstention (Q32).

The chunking A/B: re-chunk + re-embed into a parallel index, hold embedder, k, reranker, prompt, and generator constant, run the same golden set against both — retrieval metrics (recall@k/nDCG) move first and attribute the change; end-to-end faithfulness confirms it mattered.
Treat the golden set as a living asset: version it, grow it from production failures (every bad answer becomes a test case), and refresh as the corpus drifts.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_rag Q45 · S12 Production RAG Systems) "Six months live, no deploys, and users say answers got worse. What drifted — and what monitoring would have caught it before the complaints?
points: The drift suspects: corpus drift (documents grew, aged, contradicted each other; ingestion quietly failing on a new document format — check indexing lag and error rates from Q7), query drift (users now ask about topics/products the golden set never covered — new-intent clusters with poor retrieval), and relevance drift (yesterday's correct answer is stale today even though retrieval is "right").

What catches it: continuous scoring of sampled production traffic — the reference-free triad metrics (Q39) on a sample of real queries, trended weekly; falling faithfulness or context relevance is the alarm that precedes complaints.

Cheap leading indicators to dashboard: retrieval score distributions (top-1 similarity drifting down = queries leaving the index's coverage), abstention/"not found" rate, per-stage latency, citation-click and thumbs-down rates, and golden-set re-runs on a schedule — if the frozen system's score on a refreshed eval set falls, the world moved.

Attribution machinery: per-stage tracing (Q31) so a bad sampled answer decomposes into rewrite/retrieval/assembly/generation blame in minutes; user feedback wired into the eval set so every complaint becomes a permanent regression test.

Close the loop like an owner: drift monitoring feeds a standing cadence — re-curate the corpus, refresh the golden set, revisit re-embedding (Q44) — and an honest cost trend review, because token spend drifts up with corpus and traffic too. Perpetual degradation-by-default is the argument that RAG is an operated system, not a shipped feature — and if the team can't staff that, that's the real build-vs-buy input.
